L18@P0: Wright (2014) recently presented a survey of sporting rules from an Operational Research (OR) perspective. He surveyed 21 sports, which consider the rules of sports and tournaments and whether changes
L19@P0: have led to unintended consequences. The paper concludes: “Overall, it would seem that this is just a
L20@P0: taster and there may be plenty more such studies to come”. In this paper we present one such study.
L21@P0: This is an interdisciplinary paper, which cuts across economics, sport and Operational Research. We
L22@P0: recognize that the paper could have been published in any of these disciplines but for the sake of continuity with the paper that motivated this study, we wanted to publish this paper in an OR journal.
L23@P0: We look at specific examples where the rules of sports have led to unforeseen and/or unwanted consequences. We hope that the paper will be especially useful to sports administrators, helping them to
L24@P0: review what has not previously worked and also encouraging them to engage with the scientific community when considering making changes.
L25@P0: We believe that this is the first time that such a comprehensive review of sporting rules, which have
L26@P0: led to unexpected consequences, has been published in the scientific literature.

L28@P0: 1. Introduction
L29@P0: Wright (2014) recently published an invited review which looks
L30@P0: at sporting rules from the perspective of Operational Research
L31@P0: (OR). He considered 21 sports, carrying out a post-hoc analysis
L32@P0: of rule changes, finding, for example, that changes in the rules of
L33@P0: volleyball did lead (as desired) to more predictable match lengths
L34@P0: but also led to more defensive play, which was unforeseen. Other
L35@P0: sports have also changed their scoring systems in a similar way.
L36@P0: These include squash, ping pong, beach volleyball, badminton,
L37@P0: lawn bowls and tennis (for example the mixed double’s final set
L38@P0: being played as a “Super-Tie Break”, sometimes referred to as a
L39@P0: “best of two” format).
L40@P0: It might be assumed that rules for a given sport remain relatively static. This might be true for many sports, but for some
L41@P0: sports rules change almost every year. The Australian Football
L42@P0: League is one such example. Fig. 11, shows that in the first two
L43@P0: decades following the formation of their Rules Committee in 1994,
L44@P0: 51 rule changes were made, with only 2010 having no changes.

L50@P0: This compares to only 17 rule changes over the previous 20 years
L51@P0: (1974–1993), with 12 years seeing no changes. We suspect that
L52@P0: some changes were necessitated by unintended consequences of
L53@P0: earlier rule changes. An example is the 2006 changes which allowed a player taking a kick-out from a behind to proceed without
L54@P0: waiting for the goal umpire to finish waving his/her flags. We believe this caused the frequency of rushed behinds (exhibiting negative play) to increase over the following two years, culminating
L55@P0: in Hawthorn’s 11 rushed behinds in their 2008 Grand Final defeat of Geelong. This resulted in a rule change in 2009 preventing
L56@P0: rushed behinds unless under immediate pressure from an opposition player. Other rule changes were also due to the fact that the
L57@P0: Australian Football Council was disbanded and the AFL Rules Committee came into existence and started a series of rule changes
L58@P0: to both clean up, and speed up, the game2. We note that under
L59@P0: the Australian Football Council governance structure, rule changes
L60@P0: were harder to pass because it required a double-majority vote.
L61@P0: There is nothing to suggest that the number of rule changes in the
L62@P0: AFL will decrease3.
L63@P0: Wright (2014) suggested that further studies may be possible
L64@P0: and this paper is one such study that considers specific examples
L65@P0: from a number of sports to see where rules had unintended con2 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laws_of_Australian_rules_football.

L75@P1: (which cuts across economics, sport and OR) makes a contribution
L76@P1: to all these areas but, more importantly, it will enable the community to further study games, incentives and strategies in what
L77@P1: is a highly competitive environment. Furthermore, the pitfalls of
L78@P1: sports rules provide useful analogies to policymakers, highlighting
L79@P1: the importance of effective public policy design to improve societal
L80@P1: and economic outcomes by circumventing perverse incentives and
L81@P1: other suboptimal characteristics.
L82@P1: We also recognize that administrators have competing objectives (provide entertainment, ensure the sport is profitable, develop the sport etc.), whereas a single athlete’s aim is typically to
L83@P1: win. Athletes will also want to set records, feature in the record
L84@P1: books, become recognized by the public, develop contracts with
L85@P1: commercial companies etc., but all of these are dependent on them
L86@P1: winning, even if this is to the detriment of other objectives, such
L87@P1: as entertaining the crowd. Some athletes may want to play more
L88@P1: attractively, but may also have the attitude that it is the administrators’ responsibility to set the right incentives for them to do so,
L89@P1: allowing them to satisfy this objective while seeking to simultaneously satisfy their own. This can raise tensions in areas such as
L90@P1: tanking (the act of deliberately dropping points or losing a game
L91@P1: in order to gain some other advantage) where it is seen as being
L92@P1: against the spirit of the game but does meet the objective of the
L93@P1: athlete, yet not the administrators. Examples of tanking are a feature of this paper, occurring in several sports.

L101@P1: 1.1. Structure of the paper
L102@P1: We faced a decision as to how to structure the paper. Would
L103@P1: it be best to structure the examples around particular sports (e.g.
L104@P1: badminton, football, rugby etc.), or would it be better to structure
L105@P1: it around sporting events (e.g. Olympics, World Cups etc.), even on
L106@P1: some other basis? There is no perfect answer, but we have structured the paper alphabetically by sport (Section 3), as this is likely
L107@P1: to be how the majority of readers would wish to access the paper.
L108@P1: For example, sports administrators and fans who wish to focus on
L109@P1: a particular sport. Where necessary, we have cross-referenced material to provide access to related material. In Section 4 we have
L110@P1: provided examples (salary caps, player drafts and tournament formats), which cut across a number of sports for which we felt that
L111@P1: it would not be sensible to split into specific sports.
L112@P1: 2. Related work
L113@P1: This paper considers the unexpected consequences of when
L114@P1: rules are either changed, or when existing rules lead to unforeseen
L115@P1: events due to specific, and often unusual, circumstances. Lack of
L116@P1: rules, for a given situation, could also be problematic. One of the
L117@P1: reasons why rule changes can lead to situations in which the administrators and supporters would prefer not to happen is that it
L118@P1: is difficult to trial changes in practice. Even if they could be tested,
L119@P1: it is unlikely that all rogue cases would be revealed. However, it is
L120@P1: not always the case that the effect of possible rule changes cannot
L121@P1: be studied, at least statistically, to provide some level of confidence
L122@P1: that a rule change would have. In this related work, we draw out
L123@P1: some of the studies that have been reported in the scientific literature studying rule changes. We would also refer the reader to
L124@P1: Wright (2014) for more examples.
L125@P1: Lenten and Winchester (2015) studied (competition) bonus
L126@P1: points in Super Rugby. Some sports do not just attribute winning
L127@P1: with being the primary consideration, but the margin of the win
L128@P1: (or achieving a certain scoring outcome) may lead to bonus points.
L129@P1-2: These rules are designed to motivate more attacking play, leadingG. Kendall, L.J.A. Lenten / European Journal of Operational Research 257 (2017) 377–394 379
L130@P2: to more excitement for the supporters. Lenten and Winchester
L131@P2: refer to this as a secondary reward. They studied the last eight
L132@P2: minutes to see if playing behavior changed. They concluded that it
L133@P2: did, and in a way that was seen as favorable by the administrators.
L134@P2: They further conclude that the Six Nations Championship and
L135@P2: Australia’s National Rugby League could also benefit from a similar
L136@P2: bonus points system due to a decline in the number of tries in
L137@P2: these competitions. The paper concluded by saying: “... the results
L138@P2: show how the awarding of league points can, to a degree, be used to
L139@P2: alter tactics in ways deemed favorable by administrators.”
L140@P2: Penalty shootouts in football are seen by many as an unacceptable way to end a football match, leading to cautious play during extra time. Lenten, Libich, and Stehlík (2013) suggest that a
L141@P2: shootout could alternatively be held before extra time, with the
L142@P2: result determining the match winner only if the subsequent extra time fails to deliver a result. Their inference is that this would
L143@P2: result in more attacking play during extra time. Of course, to see
L144@P2: the results of these proposed changes would require empirical evidence by actually introducing the rule in a live (and probably more
L145@P2: than one) competition, but their binary-response models using existing match data robustly estimate that the odds of scoring in extra time would increase three-fold, with the FIFA World Cup and
L146@P2: the UEFA club competitions having a probable increase in scoring
L147@P2: outcomes of 45–60 percent.
L148@P2: One of the challenges in generating a set of fixtures is to create a schedule that is seen to be fair both before and after the
L149@P2: games are played. The OR literature has many examples that report how sports schedules can be generated (e.g. Bartsch, Drexl, &
L150@P2: Kröger, 2006; Croce & Oliveri, 2006; Goossens & Spieksma, 2012;
L151@P2: Kendall, 2008; Rasmussen, 2008; Wright, 2006). As a demonstration of the importance of the schedule to the underlying economics, Lenten (2015) considers the bias of the schedules for the
L152@P2: 2002–2011 National Football League (NFL) seasons and modifies a
L153@P2: recently introduced model (Lenten, 2011) to provide an assessment
L154@P2: of how these (unbalanced) scheduling biases affect the competitive balance of such leagues. There are several surveys available
L155@P2: (e.g. Kendall, Knust, Ribeiro, & Urrutia, 2010; Rasmussen & Trick,
L156@P2: 2008; Ribeiro, 2012; Wright, 2009) on sports scheduling which,
L157@P2: some would argue, is one of the most important aspects of designing fair sporting competitions.
